newsitem.title: UK: Incredulous N.Ireland welcomes Orange move.
newsitem.headline: Incredulous N.Ireland welcomes Orange move.

text.p: Hungry, fat and fourteen, one of Northern Ireland's next generation of Protestants said he was "gobsmacked" by the Orange Order's decision to cancel parades that their ancestors would never have abandoned.
"You're joking me. It's not true," said the youth, gathered with some pals under the light of an all-night shop to feast on soft drinks and sweets on a humid, historic night in Belfast.

A gleaming red saloon car drove up to the shop. Out stepped two members of the current Protestant generation, on-duty policemen, revolvers holstered and wearing flak jackets after a week of violent Catholic unrest and IRA sniper attacks.

All week they had been in the frontline against Catholics throwing petrol bombs and rocks to protest against marches on the "Glorious 12th of July," the highlight of the Protestant marching season which is marked by huge bonfires and parties.

"How's the bonnie (bonfire) going, lads?" one policeman asked the youths, gesturing to a stretch of waste land in the city centre where a bonfire the height of a small high-rise building was visible under the city's Orange night lights.
"It's going to be great. It's huge, they'll see it in Londonderry," replied another youth, referring to the Catholic nationalist stronghold 80 miles (120 km) away.
"Great," replied the policeman. "But you know there'll be no parades this year. They've called them off just now. No parade down the Lower Ormeau Road, nothing. It's all off."

The reaction of the gang of four was typical of that of many who awoke on Friday morning to hear or read that for the first time in living memory, "The Orange" would not be marching on many of its most hallowed routes on Saturday.
"They never agreed that. I don't believe you. It's not true," said another of the youths through a mouthful of crisps. "They never gave in to those taig bastards."

Taig is the derogatory word Protestants use for the 40 per cent Catholic minority whose dreams of reuniting the province with Ireland are anathema to the Orange Order, which wants it to remain for ever British.
"Yes it's true lad," replied the policeman. "They did it to stop any more trouble. So enjoy your bonnie, but there'll be no parades," he said.
The youths were dumbstruck. The policeman sensed their bewilderment and came back to explain the reality in terms that they could understand.
"You see," he said, moderating his authoritarian tone to something more avuncular, "it's like this. The Orange have really stuck it to the Nationalists."
"They's told the Nationalists the ball is in their court. They've said okay, we won't march, so what are youse (you) going to do for us. Are you gonna give us peace or what?"
It was an argument being rehearsed in many Protestant households and on the airwaves of a province abuzz with speculation about something it had thought unthinkable.

Sinn Fein, the political wing of IRA guerrillas fighting British rule of Northern Ireland, had demanded a ban on the parades as a sign that Britain's new Labour would be even-handed with Protestants and Catholics.

Its leadership has hinted that, in return, the IRA might declare the ceasefire that would earn it a seat at Northern Ireland peace talks to negotiate a lasting settlement to a conflict that has killed 3,200.

The two policemen returned to their car and disappeared in the direction of Catholic West Belfast, whose streets near witness to the biggest eruption of Catholic anger since civil rights marches in the 1970s at the start "The Troubles."
The 2,000 rubber bullets fired by police to contain riots have vanished, now collectors' items, but the twisted hulks of burned out vehicles hijacked by rioters still litter streets.
"Taig bastards," repeated one of the older boys, trying out the policeman's theory. "We've really shown them then, haven't we?"
